displayQuote: You must never be fearful about what you are doing when it is right

meta.title: Who really said "You must never be fearful about what you are doing when it is right"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Everyone credits Rosa Parks, and nobody says where. What the archives do and do not show about one of her most reproduced lines.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'You must never be fearful about what you are doing when it is right'?
meta.ogDescription: Attributed to Rosa Parks everywhere, sourced nowhere — not in Wikiquote, not in her digitised papers. Here is what we could and could not establish.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: The line is credited to Parks consistently and, as far as we can tell, only ever to Parks — there is no rival claimant and nothing about it is out of character. What is missing is a source. We could not find it in her books, in the digitised Rosa Parks Papers, or in Wikiquote’s sourced list, so we credit it to her without claiming she is documented saying it.

source.heading: Where it comes from

docMeta.dd: Quotation collections and reproductions; none names an occasion

source.excerpt: You must never be fearful about what you are doing when it is right.
trail: It is not on Wikiquote’s Rosa Parks page at all. The Rosa Parks article ↗ carries a sourced quotation list — Rosa Parks: My Story, an NPR interview, her 1995 Washington speech, the Quiet Strength section — and this line appears in none of it, neither as sourced nor as disputed. For a quotation this widely reproduced, absence from the specialist page is meaningful.
Quote Investigator has never taken it up. A site search of quoteinvestigator.com ↗ returns no article on this wording. QI has not confirmed it and has not debunked it; it simply has not been traced.

The Library of Congress holds her papers, and the phrase is not in them. A full-text search of the digitised Rosa Parks Papers returns no hit for “never be fearful” ↗; the only document in the collection matching the word fearful at all is her 1978 interview for Radcliffe’s Black Women Oral History Project, which does not contain this sentence. That is not proof she never said it — the collection is large and not everything she said was written down — but it is where a documented version should have surfaced.

What does exist under her name is art, not evidence. The Library of Congress catalogues a colour letterpress print titled with this sentence ↗, made around 2018 by the artist Amos Paul Kennedy, Jr. as part of a Rosa Parks series he began after her death in 2005. It shows the line circulating under her name a decade after she died. It does not show where it started.
source.excerptNote: Reproduced as it circulates. No longer passage, and no surrounding context, could be located — which is itself part of the problem.
source.rightsNote: We could not identify the work this wording first appeared in, so there is no rights status to give — and it is certainly not public domain. Parks died in 2005 and everything she published appeared long after 1930, so if the line is hers, it belongs to her estate and whichever publisher first printed it. Credit her as shown, but get permission before commercial or published reuse.

author.name: Rosa Parks
author.heading: About Rosa Parks
author.bio: Born Rosa Louise McCauley in Tuskegee, Alabama, Parks was a trained NAACP organiser and its Montgomery branch secretary long before 1 December 1955, when she refused to give up her bus seat and set the Montgomery bus boycott in motion. She spent the rest of her life — most of it in Detroit, where she worked for Congressman John Conyers — insisting that the moment was the result of organising, not of tired feet. She died in Detroit in 2005.

context.heading: Why this one is worth pausing on
lead: Parks spent the last fifty years of her life correcting the record about herself — insisting she was not simply tired, that she was a trained organiser, that the boycott was planned work rather than one woman’s spontaneous mood. It is a particular irony that the lines most often put in her mouth are the ones nobody can source.

This one may well be hers. Nothing about it is implausible, no one else claims it, and a life that public generates more sayings than any archive catches. But “sounds like her” is how quotations get built, not how they get verified, and on a woman who cared this much about accurate attribution it is worth saying plainly which one we have.
context.pull: Sounds like her is how quotations get built, not how they get verified.
